sections.heading: What you're looking at
sections.body: Sultanganj Bronze Buddha is a celebrated work from c. 500–700 CE, created in lost-wax cast copper / bronze (500 kg) by Post-Gupta / Early Pala Transition artisans.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Discovered and catalogued by Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery, this piece stands as a masterwork reflecting the social, spiritual, and technical achievements of its civilization.

lookCloser: Notice the fine craftsmanship and symmetry preserved across centuries.
Observe the distinctive textures and gestures that give this piece its expressive life.

claims.span: Cast in copper using the lost-wax technique, weighing more than 500 kilograms.
Stands 2.3 metres (7.5 feet) high as the largest surviving complete metal Indian statue of its antiquity.
Discovered in 1861 during railway excavation at Sultanganj, Bihar by engineer E. B. Harris.
Exported to England in 1864 and placed in the Birmingham Museum collection.
Dated to circa 500–700 CE during the transition between the Gupta and early Pala periods.
The right hand displays Abhaya Mudra (protection) while the left hand holds the folded robe hem.
